Advantages of CNC Technology Applications of CNC Technology in Manufacturing CNC Machine Technology Industrial CNC Technology CNC Technology Services Future Trends in CNC Technology Conclusion CNC technology plays a strategic role in modern manufacturing ecosystems by enabling scalable, automated, and data-driven production across multiple industries. Rather than focusing on individual machines, CNC technology connects digital design, machining processes, and quality systems into an integrated manufacturing workflow. This allows manufacturers to achieve higher throughput, tighter tolerances, and more predictable production outcomes across the entire product lifecycle. By integrating digital design files with computer-controlled machinery, CNC systems allow manufacturers to produce complex parts with consistent accuracy, scalability, and efficiency. From prototyping to full-scale industrial production, CNC technology supports faster workflows, tighter tolerances, and seamless coordination between design, machining, and quality control. For readers who want a clear definition of CNC and a foundational explanation of how CNC machines operate, we provide a dedicated CNC meaning and definition guide that focuses specifically on terminology and basic concepts. To translate CNC technology into real manufacturing outcomes, professional machining services play a critical role. JLCCNC provides CNC machining solutions that support prototyping, small-batch production, and industrial-scale manufacturing, enabling companies to apply CNC technology efficiently without investing in in-house capacity. What is CNC Technology? CNC technology refers to the integrated use of software, control systems, and automated machinery to manage and execute precision manufacturing processes. In modern production environments, CNC technology functions as a core manufacturing platform—linking digital design data with machining operations, tool management, and quality control systems. Advantages of CNC Technology CNC technology offers a wide range of advantages that make it essential to modern manufacturing. By combining computer-controlled automation with high-performance machinery, CNC systems significantly improve manufacturing efficiency. They also enable superior quality and scalability across diverse industries. High Precision and Consistent Accuracy One of the most significant advantages of CNC technology is its ability to deliver extremely high precision. CNC technology can repeatedly produce components with tight tolerances that are difficult or impossible to achieve through manual machining. Once a program is validated, the same dimensions and surface quality can be maintained across thousands of parts, ensuring consistent accuracy even in complex geometries. This level of precision is especially critical in industries such as aerospace, automotive, medical devices, and electronics, where small dimensional deviations can affect performance, safety, or compliance with industry standards. Increased Production Efficiency CNC technology dramatically improves production efficiency by automating machining operations. Machines can run continuously with minimal operator intervention, reducing setup time and accelerating production cycles. Multi-axis CNC systems further enhance efficiency by completing multiple operations—such as milling, drilling, and contouring—in a single setup. Automated tool changes, optimized tool paths, and high-speed machining capabilities allow manufacturers to shorten lead times and respond quickly to changing production demands. Excellent Repeatability and Quality Control Repeatability is a core strength of CNC technology. Every part produced from the same CNC program is virtually identical, minimizing variation and reducing scrap rates. This repeatability simplifies quality control processes, as fewer manual inspections are required once a process is stabilized. CNC systems also integrate easily with in-process measurement and inspection technologies, enabling real-time quality monitoring and early detection of deviations before defects occur. Material and Design Versatility CNC technology supports a wide range of materials, including metals, plastics, composites, and engineered alloys. From aluminum and stainless steel to advanced polymers and titanium, CNC machines can be optimized to handle different cutting characteristics and surface finish requirements. A common example is aluminum CNC machining , which is widely used due to aluminum’s excellent machinability and strength-to-weight ratio. In addition, CNC technology enables the machining of complex shapes, internal features, and intricate contours that would be extremely time-consuming or impractical with conventional methods. This design freedom allows engineers to innovate without being limited by manufacturing constraints. Scalability from Prototyping to Mass Production Another key advantage of CNC technology is its scalability. The same CNC setup can be used for rapid prototyping, small-batch production, and high-volume manufacturing with minimal modification. Design changes can be implemented quickly by updating the digital program rather than retooling entire production lines. This flexibility is particularly valuable for startups, R&D teams, and manufacturers operating in fast-moving markets where product iterations are frequent. Reduced Labor Dependency and Improved Safety By automating machining tasks, CNC technology reduces reliance on manual labor and lowers the risk of human error. Operators are less exposed to cutting tools and moving machine components, resulting in a safer working environment. Modern CNC systems also feature built-in safety controls, error detection, and machine monitoring functions that further protect both personnel and equipment while maintaining stable production. Cost Efficiency Over the Product Lifecycle While CNC machines require an initial investment, they offer long-term cost advantages. Reduced material waste, lower rework rates, shorter production times, and improved machine utilization all contribute to a lower cost per part over the product lifecycle. For manufacturers seeking consistent quality, predictable output, and efficient resource usage, CNC technology represents a cost-effective solution that supports sustainable growth. Applications of CNC Technology in Manufacturing CNC technology has a wide range of applications across industries due to its ability to deliver high precision, consistency, and production efficiency. From large-scale industrial manufacturing to rapid prototyping, CNC technology continues to expand as materials, software, and machine capabilities evolve. Applications in Metalworking CNC milling machines, lathes, and laser cutters handle metals like aluminum, steel, and titanium with unmatched precision. These machines reduce manual labor, minimize errors, and allow for complex shapes that meet rigorous industry standards. In metalworking industries where tolerance control and material consistency are critical, CNC technology enables reliable production of complex metal components at scale. Applications in Plastics and Woodworking Beyond metals, CNC routers can cut, engrave, and shape plastic components or wood panels with high accuracy. Routers are typically used for wood and plastic materials, while milling machines are better suited for metal machining due to their rigidity and cutting capabilities. Manufacturers can efficiently produce prototypes and mass-produced items, lowering production costs and turnaround times. Industrial Applications Industries such as automotive, aerospace, electronics, energy, and heavy machinery rely on CNC systems to produce structural components, housings, brackets, and precision parts. CNC machining ensures tight tolerances, repeatability, and high reliability for critical components. Prototyping and Small Batch Production Rapid prototyping and small-batch CNC production allow engineers to quickly transform digital designs into functional prototypes, enabling faster design validation, iterative testing, and reduced time-to-market. Innovative Uses in Various Industries Advanced applications such as multi-axis cutting, hybrid additive-subtractive manufacturing, and complex 3D contour machining expand possibilities in medical devices, architecture, and custom design. CNC Machine Technology Types of CNC Machines CNC machine technology includes milling machines, lathes, routers, plasma cutters, and laser engraving systems. Each type serves a specific function, from cutting and drilling to shaping and engraving, meeting diverse manufacturing needs. How CNC Machines Work CNC machines operate by translating digital designs into precise machining actions through integrated control systems. This enables highly accurate and repeatable production while minimizing material waste and optimizing workflow efficiency. Maintenance and Optimization Proper maintenance of CNC machines is essential for long-term performance. Regular calibration, tool replacement, and software updates optimize machine efficiency and prevent downtime. Skilled operators can further enhance productivity by choosing the right tooling and machining parameters. Industrial CNC Technology Automation in Large-Scale Production Industrial CNC technology enables full automation of production lines. Large-scale manufacturing can run continuously with minimal human supervision, improving throughput and reducing labor costs. Integration with Industrial Processes CNC technology integrates seamlessly with industrial processes such as assembly, quality inspection, and material handling. This integration allows for smarter factories, streamlined workflows, and higher overall efficiency. Case Studies Industries adopting industrial CNC technology have reported reduced production errors, faster turnaround times, and improved product consistency. For example, automotive suppliers use CNC machines to produce engine components with precise tolerances, enhancing vehicle performance and reliability. CNC Technology Services Design and Consulting Services CNC technology services extend beyond machining itself. Design and consulting services help manufacturers apply CNC technology effectively by optimizing material selection, machining strategies, and process planning before production begins. Manufacturing and Prototyping Services Service providers offer CNC machining for both prototypes and mass production. This allows businesses to outsource specialized tasks, reduce overhead, and maintain high-quality standards. Maintenance and Support Services Many CNC technology service providers also offer ongoing maintenance, troubleshooting, and training. This ensures clients can maintain efficient operations, extend machine lifespan, and minimize production delays. Future Trends in CNC Technology Beyond basic CNC operation and machine control, future CNC technology development is increasingly driven by intelligence, connectivity, and system-level integration. Future developments will not only improve precision and productivity but also fundamentally reshape how factories operate, how products are designed, and how manufacturers compete in global markets. Smart CNC and AI Integration The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with CNC systems is transforming machining from reactive automation into predictive and adaptive manufacturing. AI-powered algorithms can analyze historical machining data. They automatically optimize tool paths, reduce cycle times, and minimize tool wear. Machine learning models are increasingly used to detect subtle signs of tool degradation or misalignment before they cause defects. In aerospace and medical device manufacturing, where tolerances are extremely tight, AI-assisted CNC tool path optimization is already being adopted to ensure consistency and precision across complex geometries. Over time, smart CNC machines will be able to adjust cutting strategies in real time, self-correcting for material inconsistencies and dynamic load variations without human intervention. IoT and Connected Manufacturing The rise of the Internet of Things (IoT) enables CNC machines to become integral components of connected smart factories. Sensors embedded in CNC equipment collect real-time data on temperature, vibration, spindle load, and tool life. This data, streamed through secure networks, feeds into centralized manufacturing execution systems (MES) and enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems to support real-time monitoring and informed decision-making. Connected CNC machines can automatically schedule maintenance based on actual usage patterns, reducing unplanned downtime. In facilities with multiple machines producing different parts, IoT connectivity enhances workflow coordination, material tracking, and quality control, leading to higher operational efficiency and lower production costs. Advanced Materials and Machining Techniques As new materials continue to emerge, CNC technology evolves to address the challenges they present. Advanced composites, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) , and next-generation polymers have unique machining requirements. High-entropy alloys are composed of multiple principal elements in near-equal proportions, offering exceptional strength, wear resistance, and thermal stability. These materials are increasingly used in aerospace and energy applications, where CNC machining must precisely control cutting forces and heat generation to maintain part integrity. CNC technology is also incorporating hybrid manufacturing techniques that combine additive manufacturing (3D printing) with traditional subtractive machining. These hybrid processes allow complex internal structures to be built additively and then finished with high-precision CNC cutting, making them ideal for lightweight aerospace components and customized medical implants. Human–Machine Collaboration and Augmented Reality Future CNC environments will emphasize human–machine collaboration, where operators work alongside intelligent machining systems rather than simply monitoring them. Augmented reality (AR) tools will support setup, training, and maintenance by overlaying digital instructions directly onto physical machinery. Technicians wearing AR headsets will be guided step-by-step through complex calibration or repair processes, reducing training time and lowering the risk of error. Furthermore, virtual simulation environments will allow engineers to preview machining operations before any material is cut. This not only helps validate designs but also ensures that tooling and fixturing are optimized for efficiency and safety. Conclusion Summary of Key Benefits CNC technology has transformed modern manufacturing by improving precision, efficiency, and flexibility. It enables complex machining, reduces errors, and accelerates production cycles. Impact on Modern Manufacturing With industrial CNC technology, advanced machines, and comprehensive services, manufacturers can achieve high-quality output, innovate rapidly, and maintain a competitive edge. As CNC technology continues to evolve, its influence on the manufacturing industry will only grow stronger. Advantages of CNC Technology Applications of CNC Technology in Manufacturing CNC Machine Technology Industrial CNC Technology CNC Technology Services Future Trends in CNC Technology Conclusion CNC technology plays a strategic role in modern manufacturing ecosystems by enabling scalable, automated, and data-driven production across multiple industries. Rather than focusing on individual machines, CNC technology connects digital design, machining processes, and quality systems into an integrated manufacturing workflow. This allows manufacturers to achieve higher throughput, tighter tolerances, and more predictable production outcomes across the entire product lifecycle. By integrating digital design files with computer-controlled machinery, CNC systems allow manufacturers to produce complex parts with consistent accuracy, scalability, and efficiency. From prototyping to full-scale industrial production, CNC technology supports faster workflows, tighter tolerances, and seamless coordination between design, machining, and quality control. For readers who want a clear definition of CNC and a foundational explanation of how CNC machines operate, we provide a dedicated CNC meaning and definition guide that focuses specifically on terminology and basic concepts. To translate CNC technology into real manufacturing outcomes, professional machining services play a critical role. JLCCNC provides CNC machining solutions that support prototyping, small-batch production, and industrial-scale manufacturing, enabling companies to apply CNC technology efficiently without investing in in-house capacity. What is CNC Technology? CNC technology refers to the integrated use of software, control systems, and automated machinery to manage and execute precision manufacturing processes. In modern production environments, CNC technology functions as a core manufacturing platform—linking digital design data with machining operations, tool management, and quality control systems. Advantages of CNC Technology CNC technology offers a wide range of advantages that make it essential to modern manufacturing. By combining computer-controlled automation with high-performance machinery, CNC systems significantly improve manufacturing efficiency. They also enable superior quality and scalability across diverse industries. High Precision and Consistent Accuracy One of the most significant advantages of CNC technology is its ability to deliver extremely high precision. CNC technology can repeatedly produce components with tight tolerances that are difficult or impossible to achieve through manual machining. Once a program is validated, the same dimensions and surface quality can be maintained across thousands of parts, ensuring consistent accuracy even in complex geometries. This level of precision is especially critical in industries such as aerospace, automotive, medical devices, and electronics, where small dimensional deviations can affect performance, safety, or compliance with industry standards. Increased Production Efficiency CNC technology dramatically improves production efficiency by automating machining operations. Machines can run continuously with minimal operator intervention, reducing setup time and accelerating production cycles. Multi-axis CNC systems further enhance efficiency by completing multiple operations—such as milling, drilling, and contouring—in a single setup. Automated tool changes, optimized tool paths, and high-speed machining capabilities allow manufacturers to shorten lead times and respond quickly to changing production demands. Excellent Repeatability and Quality Control Repeatability is a core strength of CNC technology. Every part produced from the same CNC program is virtually identical, minimizing variation and reducing scrap rates. This repeatability simplifies quality control processes, as fewer manual inspections are required once a process is stabilized. CNC systems also integrate easily with in-process measurement and inspection technologies, enabling real-time quality monitoring and early detection of deviations before defects occur. Material and Design Versatility CNC technology supports a wide range of materials, including metals, plastics, composites, and engineered alloys. From aluminum and stainless steel to advanced polymers and titanium, CNC machines can be optimized to handle different cutting characteristics and surface finish requirements. A common example is aluminum CNC machining , which is widely used due to aluminum’s excellent machinability and strength-to-weight ratio. In addition, CNC technology enables the machining of complex shapes, internal features, and intricate contours that would be extremely time-consuming or impractical with conventional methods. This design freedom allows engineers to innovate without being limited by manufacturing constraints. Scalability from Prototyping to Mass Production Another key advantage of CNC technology is its scalability. The same CNC setup can be used for rapid prototyping, small-batch production, and high-volume manufacturing with minimal modification. Design changes can be implemented quickly by updating the digital program rather than retooling entire production lines. This flexibility is particularly valuable for startups, R&D teams, and manufacturers operating in fast-moving markets where product iterations are frequent. Reduced Labor Dependency and Improved Safety By automating machining tasks, CNC technology reduces reliance on manual labor and lowers the risk of human error. Operators are less exposed to cutting tools and moving machine components, resulting in a safer working environment. Modern CNC systems also feature built-in safety controls, error detection, and machine monitoring functions that further protect both personnel and equipment while maintaining stable production. Cost Efficiency Over the Product Lifecycle While CNC machines require an initial investment, they offer long-term cost advantages. Reduced material waste, lower rework rates, shorter production times, and improved machine utilization all contribute to a lower cost per part over the product lifecycle. For manufacturers seeking consistent quality, predictable output, and efficient resource usage, CNC technology represents a cost-effective solution that supports sustainable growth. Applications of CNC Technology in Manufacturing CNC technology has a wide range of applications across industries due to its ability to deliver high precision, consistency, and production efficiency. From large-scale industrial manufacturing to rapid prototyping, CNC technology continues to expand as materials, software, and machine capabilities evolve. Applications in Metalworking CNC milling machines, lathes, and laser cutters handle metals like aluminum, steel, and titanium with unmatched precision. These machines reduce manual labor, minimize errors, and allow for complex shapes that meet rigorous industry standards. In metalworking industries where tolerance control and material consistency are critical, CNC technology enables reliable production of complex metal components at scale. Applications in Plastics and Woodworking Beyond metals, CNC routers can cut, engrave, and shape plastic components or wood panels with high accuracy. Routers are typically used for wood and plastic materials, while milling machines are better suited for metal machining due to their rigidity and cutting capabilities. Manufacturers can efficiently produce prototypes and mass-produced items, lowering production costs and turnaround times. Industrial Applications Industries such as automotive, aerospace, electronics, energy, and heavy machinery rely on CNC systems to produce structural components, housings, brackets, and precision parts. CNC machining ensures tight tolerances, repeatability, and high reliability for critical components. Prototyping and Small Batch Production Rapid prototyping and small-batch CNC production allow engineers to quickly transform digital designs into functional prototypes, enabling faster design validation, iterative testing, and reduced time-to-market. Innovative Uses in Various Industries Advanced applications such as multi-axis cutting, hybrid additive-subtractive manufacturing, and complex 3D contour machining expand possibilities in medical devices, architecture, and custom design. CNC Machine Technology Types of CNC Machines CNC machine technology includes milling machines, lathes, routers, plasma cutters, and laser engraving systems. Each type serves a specific function, from cutting and drilling to shaping and engraving, meeting diverse manufacturing needs. How CNC Machines Work CNC machines operate by translating digital designs into precise machining actions through integrated control systems. This enables highly accurate and repeatable production while minimizing material waste and optimizing workflow efficiency. Maintenance and Optimization Proper maintenance of CNC machines is essential for long-term performance. Regular calibration, tool replacement, and software updates optimize machine efficiency and prevent downtime. Skilled operators can further enhance productivity by choosing the right tooling and machining parameters. Industrial CNC Technology Automation in Large-Scale Production Industrial CNC technology enables full automation of production lines. Large-scale manufacturing can run continuously with minimal human supervision, improving throughput and reducing labor costs. Integration with Industrial Processes CNC technology integrates seamlessly with industrial processes such as assembly, quality inspection, and material handling. This integration allows for smarter factories, streamlined workflows, and higher overall efficiency. Case Studies Industries adopting industrial CNC technology have reported reduced production errors, faster turnaround times, and improved product consistency. For example, automotive suppliers use CNC machines to produce engine components with precise tolerances, enhancing vehicle performance and reliability. CNC Technology Services Design and Consulting Services CNC technology services extend beyond machining itself. Design and consulting services help manufacturers apply CNC technology effectively by optimizing material selection, machining strategies, and process planning before production begins. Manufacturing and Prototyping Services Service providers offer CNC machining for both prototypes and mass production. This allows businesses to outsource specialized tasks, reduce overhead, and maintain high-quality standards. Maintenance and Support Services Many CNC technology service providers also offer ongoing maintenance, troubleshooting, and training. This ensures clients can maintain efficient operations, extend machine lifespan, and minimize production delays. Future Trends in CNC Technology Beyond basic CNC operation and machine control, future CNC technology development is increasingly driven by intelligence, connectivity, and system-level integration. Future developments will not only improve precision and productivity but also fundamentally reshape how factories operate, how products are designed, and how manufacturers compete in global markets. Smart CNC and AI Integration The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with CNC systems is transforming machining from reactive automation into predictive and adaptive manufacturing. AI-powered algorithms can analyze historical machining data. They automatically optimize tool paths, reduce cycle times, and minimize tool wear. Machine learning models are increasingly used to detect subtle signs of tool degradation or misalignment before they cause defects. In aerospace and medical device manufacturing, where tolerances are extremely tight, AI-assisted CNC tool path optimization is already being adopted to ensure consistency and precision across complex geometries. Over time, smart CNC machines will be able to adjust cutting strategies in real time, self-correcting for material inconsistencies and dynamic load variations without human intervention. IoT and Connected Manufacturing The rise of the Internet of Things (IoT) enables CNC machines to become integral components of connected smart factories. Sensors embedded in CNC equipment collect real-time data on temperature, vibration, spindle load, and tool life. This data, streamed through secure networks, feeds into centralized manufacturing execution systems (MES) and enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems to support real-time monitoring and informed decision-making. Connected CNC machines can automatically schedule maintenance based on actual usage patterns, reducing unplanned downtime. In facilities with multiple machines producing different parts, IoT connectivity enhances workflow coordination, material tracking, and quality control, leading to higher operational efficiency and lower production costs. Advanced Materials and Machining Techniques As new materials continue to emerge, CNC technology evolves to address the challenges they present. Advanced composites, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) , and next-generation polymers have unique machining requirements. High-entropy alloys are composed of multiple principal elements in near-equal proportions, offering exceptional strength, wear resistance, and thermal stability. These materials are increasingly used in aerospace and energy applications, where CNC machining must precisely control cutting forces and heat generation to maintain part integrity. CNC technology is also incorporating hybrid manufacturing techniques that combine additive manufacturing (3D printing) with traditional subtractive machining. These hybrid processes allow complex internal structures to be built additively and then finished with high-precision CNC cutting, making them ideal for lightweight aerospace components and customized medical implants. Human–Machine Collaboration and Augmented Reality Future CNC environments will emphasize human–machine collaboration, where operators work alongside intelligent machining systems rather than simply monitoring them. Augmented reality (AR) tools will support setup, training, and maintenance by overlaying digital instructions directly onto physical machinery. Technicians wearing AR headsets will be guided step-by-step through complex calibration or repair processes, reducing training time and lowering the risk of error. Furthermore, virtual simulation environments will allow engineers to preview machining operations before any material is cut. This not only helps validate designs but also ensures that tooling and fixturing are optimized for efficiency and safety. Conclusion Summary of Key Benefits CNC technology has transformed modern manufacturing by improving precision, efficiency, and flexibility. It enables complex machining, reduces errors, and accelerates production cycles. Impact on Modern Manufacturing With industrial CNC technology, advanced machines, and comprehensive services, manufacturers can achieve high-quality output, innovate rapidly, and maintain a competitive edge. As CNC technology continues to evolve, its influence on the manufacturing industry will only grow stronger. Glaeser 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Glaeser 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design. Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Erik 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design. Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Each PCB has a unique function for a particular product. Therefore, producing a PCB is a complex process of many steps. This overview covers the most important steps when producing a multilayer PCB. When you order PCBs from the PCBWay, you are buying quality that pays for itself over time. This is guaranteed through a product specification and quality control that is far more stringent than other suppliers, and ensures that the product delivers what it promises. In the production flow below you can see where the PCBWay process is unique or goes beyond the IPC standard. Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. Hide Details 01-1.Preparing the phototools Artwork Master is PCB production in the key steps, which directly affect the quality of the final product quality,An accurately scaled configuration of electronic data used to produce the artwork master or production master. Artwork Master – The photographic image of the PCB pattern on film used to produce the circuit board, usually on a 1:1 scale.In general, there are three types of Artwork Master:(1) Conductive Pattern (2) solder mask (3) Silkscreen Put away 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. Hide Details 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. Hide Details 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design. Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. Hide Details 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. Hide Details 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. Hide Details 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill Hide Details 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. Hide Details 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Hide Details 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. Hide Details 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. Hide Details 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. Hide Details 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Hide Details 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. Hide Details 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. Hide Details 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. Hide Details 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. Hide Details 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill Hide Details 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. Hide Details 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Hide Details 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. Hide Details 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. Hide Details 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. Hide Details 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Hide Details 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. Hide Details 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. Hide Details 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Published Jul 29, 2025, updated Jul 28, 2025 5 min Threading a hole sounds simple, until you’re deciding between thread milling and tapping . Both methods are staples in CNC machining and manual operations, but they serve different purposes, machines, and tolerances. Whether you're threading aluminum, stainless steel, or titanium, choosing the wrong method can mean broken tools, scrapped parts, or wasted hours. Let’s break down the real differences between thread milling vs tapping , when to use one over the other, and how to choose the right tool for your part. What is Tapping? Tapping is the traditional method of creating internal threads by driving a tap, a hardened cutting tool, into a pre-drilled hole. It’s fast, easy to set up, and widely used in manual and CNC operations. There are three common types of taps: ● Hand taps – used manually with a T-handle ● Spiral point taps – best for through holes ● Spiral flute taps – best for blind holes Taps are typically specific to one thread size and pitch, which makes them convenient but rigid in flexibility.
